summary: This proposed standard describes the part of the CDNI Control interface that lets an upstream CDN trigger activity in a downstream CDN, for example to pre-position metadata or content or to remove it. It is used when the downstream CDN delivers content on the upstream CDN's behalf.

eli5.summary: A shop owner can tell a partner shop to stock up on an item or clear it off shelves. This defines how one content network sends such requests to another.

questions: how does a cdn preposition content
subtitle: How one CDN tells a partner CDN to pre-load, revalidate or delete content, and then checks on the job.

tldr.problem: When one content delivery network (the upstream CDN) hands delivery to another (the downstream CDN), it needs a standard way to ask the partner to fetch, revalidate or delete metadata and content.
tldr.mechanism: The upstream CDN POSTs a JSON command to a collection of Trigger Status Resources on the downstream CDN's web service. The downstream CDN creates a status resource, returns its location with HTTP 201, and the upstream CDN polls it.
tldr.outcome: There are three trigger types (preposition, invalidate, purge), a cancel command, defined status values and error codes, and loop prevention. This is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8007 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata it records shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the trigger part of the CDNI Control interface, alongside the metadata interface in RFC 8006.

sections.title: The CI/T Interface
sections.content:
This RFC describes the CI/T interface, short for CDNI Control interface / Triggers. It is one part of the Control interface of Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI), the framework described in RFC 6707 and RFC 7336. It does not cover configuration, bootstrapping or authentication of CDN interconnect interfaces.

The idea is simple. An upstream CDN (uCDN) has content that a downstream CDN (dCDN) delivers on its behalf. CI/T lets the uCDN ask the dCDN to pre-position metadata or content, or to invalidate or purge it, and lets the uCDN watch the progress of what it asked for.
sections.eli5: One content network owns the videos and pictures. A partner network hands them out to people. This lets the owner say "get this ready" or "throw that away" and then check whether the partner did it.

sections.title: Commands, Status Resources and Collections
sections.content:
A CI/T Command is sent from the uCDN to the dCDN. There are two kinds: a Trigger Command, and a Cancel Command that asks the dCDN to cancel an earlier Trigger Command. A Trigger Command has one of three types:

  • preposition: fetch metadata from the uCDN, or content from any origin including the uCDN.
  • invalidate: revalidate specific metadata or content before reusing it. The data need not be erased.
  • purge: delete specific metadata or content. It must not be held afterwards, but the dCDN can reacquire it from the uCDN if it needs it.

The CI/T interface is a web service offered by the dCDN, built on HTTP/1.1. When the dCDN accepts a command, it creates a Trigger Status Resource describing the triggered activity. The dCDN keeps at least one collection of these resources for each uCDN, and each uCDN can see only its own.

The dCDN may also keep optional filtered collections: pending, active, complete and failed. If it implements them, it must link to them from the collection of all Trigger Status Resources.
sections.eli5: Each request you send gets its own ticket. The partner keeps a box of tickets for you only, and you can look at a ticket any time to see how the job is going.

sections.title: Creating, Checking, Canceling and Deleting
sections.content:
To trigger activity, the uCDN POSTs a CI/T Command to the dCDN's collection of its Trigger Status Resources. A dCDN implementing CI/T must support the HTTP GET, HEAD, POST and DELETE methods. If the command is malformed or the uCDN lacks access rights, the dCDN responds with a 4xx error, or creates a "failed" status resource with an Error Description. If it accepts the command, it answers 201 with the new resource's URI in the Location header and should include the resource's content. The uCDN must not assume anything about the structure of these URIs, and the dCDN must not reuse a URI even after the resource is removed.

Status values move from pending to active to complete or failed. A dCDN that cannot track progress sets processed, meaning accepted with no further status updates. The uCDN checks progress by fetching the status resource or a collection, and should use HTTP ETags to detect change rather than refetching everything. The dCDN should use cache control headers to show how often it recommends polling.

Timing is the dCDN's choice. Invalidate and purge must apply to all data acquired before the command was accepted. If the uCDN wants to purge and then pre-position replacements at the same URLs, it should make sure the purge has finished first.

The uCDN cancels by POSTing a Cancel Command. The dCDN must answer, for example 200, 202 or 501, but actual cancellation is optional to implement. A command that cannot be stopped immediately is reported as cancelling until it stops. The uCDN can also remove a status resource at any time with DELETE. The dCDN may expire old resources, and it is recommended to keep finished ones for at least 24 hours.
sections.eli5: You hand in a request and get a receipt number. You can peek at the receipt to see if it is waiting, in progress or done, ask the partner to stop, or tear the receipt up. Stopping is polite, not guaranteed.

sections.title: Objects, Encoding and Cascades
sections.content:
All CI/T objects are JSON with the media type application/cdni and a ptype parameter: ci-trigger-command, ci-trigger-status or ci-trigger-collection. Names are lowercase and case sensitive. Unrecognized name/value pairs should be ignored and passed on in a cascade.

A command carries either trigger or cancel (exactly one), plus a mandatory cdn-path. A Trigger Specification has a type and at least one non-empty group among metadata.urls, content.urls, content.ccid, metadata.patterns and content.patterns. Pattern lists must not be used with preposition. A pattern uses an asterisk and a question mark as wildcards, with a dollar sign as the escape character, and has optional case-sensitive and match-query-string flags. URL schemes (HTTP or HTTPS) are ignored when comparing URLs.

A Trigger Status Resource holds the trigger, ctime, mtime, status, and optionally etime (the dCDN's estimated completion time) and errors. Times are seconds since the UNIX epoch, set by the dCDN, so clocks need not be synchronized.

In a cascade, an intermediate CDN must forward commands to the dCDNs that may be affected and must not report "complete" until all of them are complete. Loops are prevented with the cdn-path array. Each CDN appends its CDN Provider ID, which is AS plus its Autonomous System number, a colon and a qualifier such as AS64496:0. A dCDN must reject a command whose path already contains its own ID.
sections.eli5: Every request is written on a standard form. Each network that passes the form along signs its name on it, so if the form ever comes back to someone who already signed, they know it is going in circles.

sections.title: Errors and Failures
sections.content:
Before acceptance, the dCDN can reject a command with an HTTP status such as 400 for a malformed request, or 403 or 404 when the uCDN has no permission or is acting on another CDN's data. After acceptance, failures are listed in the errors array of the Trigger Status Resource. Each Error Description has an error code, the exact URLs or patterns it applies to (the dCDN must not generalize them) and an optional human-readable description.

If a Surrogate (a delivery cache) is offline, an invalidate may be reported complete, but the Surrogate must revalidate the data before using it again. Preposition and purge may be reported as processed and finish when the cache returns. Unknown error codes must be treated as fatal, and the request must not be retried automatically without modification.
sections.eli5: If a job goes wrong, the ticket says exactly which items failed and why, using a short code from an agreed list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
CI/T cannot read or change the metadata or content itself. It can only control whether they are present in the dCDN and the work involved. Even so, an attacker watching preposition requests could learn a uCDN's predictions of future popularity, and invalidate or purge requests could reveal catalog changes. Injected or modified commands waste the dCDN's effort and reduce its caching efficiency.

A CI/T implementation must support HTTPS (TLS) and use it with authentication of both ends, unless other protection such as an IPsec tunnel or a physically secured internal network is in place. The TLS guidance in RFC 7525 must be followed. Access control is dCDN-specific, and a dCDN must restrict each uCDN to its own data. The RFC defines no specific protection against denial of service and suggests TLS, firewalls, VPNs and rate limiting. It says the CI/T protocol carries no information about individual end users.
sections.eli5: The two networks should check each other's identity and keep the messages private. The partner should also not let one customer mess with another customer's stuff.

messages.label: POST CI/T Command
messages.note: Sent to the collection of Trigger Status Resources.

messages.label: HTTP 201
messages.note: Location header gives the new Trigger Status Resource.

items.label: processed
items.desc: Accepted, with no further status updates.

items.label: canceling
items.desc: Still in progress but canceled by the uCDN.

items.label: emeta
items.desc: The dCDN could not acquire metadata needed for the request.

items.label: econtent
items.desc: The dCDN could not acquire content (preposition only).

items.label: eperm
items.desc: The uCDN has no permission to issue the command.

items.label: ereject
items.desc: The dCDN is not willing to fulfill the command.

items.label: ecdn
items.desc: Internal error in the dCDN or one of its dCDNs.

items.label: eunsupported
items.desc: The trigger type is not supported by the dCDN.
